missions.title: Guidance Comes First

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تُقَدِّمُوا۟ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ ٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ ۖ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ  ﴿1﴾
ayahs.meaning: Believers should not put their own opinions ahead of Allah and His Messenger; they should be mindful of Allah, Who hears and knows.

options: Agree immediately so there is no disagreement.
Ask respectfully for evidence or a teacher’s guidance.
Mock the classmate for being confident.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:1    |    TRAIT: Respect for revelation • Self-control
missions.aim: Pause before claiming that your own preference is the Islamic rule. Learn to ask what Allah and His Messenger have taught.
missions.tafsir: Surah Al-Hujurat begins by calling believers to observe the authority of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Al-Tabari explains the command not to go ahead of the Messenger as refusing to put words, decisions or religious judgments before the guidance he brought. Ibn Kathir similarly treats it as a command to follow the Book and Sunnah rather than act ahead of them. The verse ends by reminding believers that Allah hears and knows. For children, the lesson is not to pretend that every personal choice is a revealed command. It is to respect authentic guidance, ask qualified adults when uncertain, and be humble enough to learn. A parent or teacher should explain that everyday matters can permit different lawful choices; the verse does not mean children must never ask questions.
missions.story: Akhlaq was helping arrange a class charity table. He wanted every child to contribute an identical amount. 'That is the only fair way,' he declared. Imaan noticed that one of their classmates had brought a handwritten kindness card instead of money. 'Could we ask the teacher what is fair?' she suggested. Akhlaq stopped. The teacher explained that charity is not a contest, and children can help according to their abilities. Afterward, Akhlaq admitted, 'I spoke as if my idea were the only right way.' Imaan replied, 'It is good to have ideas. It is even better to listen and learn before saying what Allah requires.' They welcomed the card and found a meaningful place for every child's contribution.
missions.question: A classmate says, “My preference is the only Islamic way,” without evidence. What should Imaan do?
missions.feedback: Respecting guidance includes checking evidence and speaking gently. It does not require mockery or blind agreement.
missions.action: Ask a parent or teacher one sincere question about a Sunnah you want to understand, and listen carefully to the answer.
missions.reflection: When have I spoken too confidently before learning enough?
missions.vocabulary: Taqwa — being mindful of Allah   •   Sunnah — the Prophet’s authentic way
missions.careNote: Do not present this as a ban on thoughtful questions. Separate religious rules from preferences. Do not invent a specific cause of revelation.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:1 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/1

missions.title: Words of Respect

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تَرْفَعُوٓا۟ أَصْوَٰتَكُمْ فَوْقَ صَوْتِ ٱلنَّبِىِّ وَلَا تَجْهَرُوا۟ لَهُۥ بِٱلْقَوْلِ كَجَهْرِ بَعْضِكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ أَن تَحْبَطَ أَعْمَـٰلُكُمْ وَأَنتُمْ لَا تَشْعُرُونَ  ﴿2﴾
ayahs.meaning: Believers must speak to the Prophet ﷺ with special respect, not raising their voices over his; disrespect could endanger their deeds.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَغُضُّونَ أَصْوَٰتَهُمْ عِندَ رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱمْتَحَنَ ٱللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ ۚ لَهُم مَّغْفِرَةٌ وَأَجْرٌ عَظِيمٌ  ﴿3﴾
ayahs.meaning: Those who lower their voices respectfully before Allah's Messenger have hearts tested for Taqwa and are promised forgiveness and a great reward.

options: Listen and wait for a turn to speak.
Interrupt loudly to prove you know the answer.
Ignore the lesson and joke about the Prophet ﷺ.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:2 / 49:3    |    TRAIT: Respect • Listening • Self-restraint
missions.aim: Recognize the unique status of the Prophet ﷺ and learn respectful listening as an everyday application.
missions.tafsir: These ayahs address the believers' actual etiquette toward the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. They prohibit raising voices above his and describe the virtue of lowering one's voice before him. Their primary meaning is not simply that every adult may demand unquestioning silence. Ibn Kathir discusses the seriousness of reverence for the Messenger, and the classical commentators distinguish this special prophetic respect from everyday speech. Today, children show reverence by speaking about the Prophet ﷺ honorably, listening attentively to authentic teachings, and avoiding joking disrespectfully about him. A related everyday habit is learning to wait one's turn in discussions. But the everyday exercise is an application of the verse, not a replacement for the original revelation.
missions.story: The classroom was full of excited chatter as the teacher began a lesson about the Prophet ﷺ. Akhlaq wanted to share a fact he had heard and interrupted twice. Imaan gently raised her hand instead. When the room grew quiet, the teacher explained that believers were taught special manners in the presence of Allah's Messenger. 'We cannot stand in his presence today,' she said, 'but we can honor what he taught.' Akhlaq tried again. He listened until the teacher had finished and then asked his question politely. This time the whole class heard his thoughtful contribution. He realized that speaking respectfully did not make his ideas smaller; it helped everyone learn.
missions.question: What is the most respectful response during an authentic Seerah lesson?
missions.feedback: Listening attentively and speaking respectfully honors the lesson. The original ayahs teach special respect for the Messenger ﷺ.
missions.action: During one family or class discussion today, listen without interrupting and wait for your turn.
missions.reflection: How does careful listening change the way others feel?
missions.vocabulary: Adab — good manners   •   Reverence — deep respect
missions.careNote: Do not equate the Prophet’s uniquely prescribed etiquette with unconditional obedience to any adult; children can still seek help and report mistreatment.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:2, 3 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/2

missions.title: The Gift of Patience

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يُنَادُونَكَ مِن وَرَآءِ ٱلْحُجُرَٰتِ أَكْثَرُهُمْ لَا يَعْقِلُونَ  ﴿4﴾
ayahs.meaning: Those calling out to the Prophet ﷺ loudly from outside his private rooms were showing poor understanding of proper manners.

ayahs.arabic: وَلَوْ أَنَّهُمْ صَبَرُوا۟ حَتَّىٰ تَخْرُجَ إِلَيْهِمْ لَكَانَ خَيْرًا لَّهُمْ ۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ  ﴿5﴾
ayahs.meaning: Had they patiently waited until the Prophet ﷺ came out, it would have been better; Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

options: Keep shouting until she answers.
Knock gently, wait, and return later if she is busy.
Open the door without asking.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:4 / 49:5    |    TRAIT: Patience • Privacy • Courtesy
missions.aim: Learn that others deserve private space and that waiting politely can be an act of respect.
missions.tafsir: The verses describe people calling out to the Prophet ﷺ from outside his private chambers. The Qur'an criticizes their lack of manners and says patient waiting would have been better. In Al-Tafsir al-Munir, these verses form part of the instruction to show proper adab toward Allah's Messenger. Their original setting is the Prophet's household, and this historical setting should be explained clearly. For a child's daily life, we can draw a careful practical lesson: knock before entering a room, ask at an appropriate time, and accept that someone might need rest. Children should know that an emergency is different: they may immediately call for a trusted adult when help or safety is needed.
missions.story: Akhlaq ran to Dadi Jaan's room, excited to show her a drawing. He called loudly through the door. Imaan noticed the lights were dim and remembered Dadi Jaan had been resting. 'Could we knock softly and wait?' she whispered. Akhlaq tried again, using a gentle knock. A few minutes later Dadi Jaan opened the door with a smile. 'Thank you for waiting,' she said. She enjoyed the picture, and Akhlaq listened as she told him how good manners make a home feel safe. Later, when Mohsin urgently needed help after falling outside, Akhlaq did not hesitate to call an adult. He understood that patience and respecting privacy do not mean ignoring emergencies.
missions.question: Dadi Jaan is resting behind a closed door. What should Akhlaq do?
missions.feedback: Respecting privacy and waiting are good manners. In an emergency, get help immediately.
missions.action: Knock and ask permission before entering someone’s private room once today.
missions.reflection: How would I feel if someone interrupted my rest?
missions.vocabulary: Hujurat — private rooms or chambers   •   Sabr — patient endurance
missions.careNote: Original context concerns addressing the Prophet ﷺ; modern room etiquette is an analogy. Explicit emergency exception is important.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:4, 5 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/4

missions.title: Before You Believe the News

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن جَآءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌۢ بِنَبَإٍ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓا۟ أَن تُصِيبُوا۟ قَوْمًۢا بِجَهَـٰلَةٍ فَتُصْبِحُوا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ نَـٰدِمِينَ  ﴿6﴾
ayahs.meaning: When an unreliable person brings important news, check it before acting, so that others are not harmed and you do not later regret it.

options: Forward it quickly.
Add a dramatic detail to make it interesting.
Do not share; ask a trustworthy adult to help check the facts.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:6    |    TRAIT: Truthfulness • Careful checking • Fairness
missions.aim: Learn to pause, verify important information, and avoid spreading rumors that hurt others.
missions.tafsir: Allah commands believers to investigate important reports brought by a person whose reliability is compromised, lest they harm others through ignorance and feel regret afterward. Ibn Kathir emphasizes verification before passing judgment or taking action. Classical works mention reports about circumstances of revelation; children do not need to be asked to memorize historical details whose chains may require scholarly assessment. The clear Qur'anic rule is enough: do not treat a rumor as established fact. For today's child, this applies especially to classroom gossip, group messages, copied screenshots and stories about friends. Verification should be respectful: speak to a trustworthy adult or the concerned person safely, without conducting intrusive investigations yourself.
missions.story: Someone in Akhlaq's class whispered that Mohsina had broken a library book on purpose. Soon a group message repeated the claim. Akhlaq reached for the forward button. Imaan asked, 'Do we actually know what happened?' They spoke to the librarian with their teacher. The book had fallen from a loose shelf, and Mohsina had only tried to pick it up. Akhlaq felt relieved that he had not shared the message. He thanked Imaan for helping him pause. Together they told their friends that the story had not been true, without embarrassing anyone further. The class then repaired the loose shelf. What started as gossip became a lesson in care and fairness.
missions.question: A message accuses your friend of wrongdoing, but nobody has evidence. What is safest?
missions.feedback: A pause can prevent harm. Fairness requires more than repeating what someone else said.
missions.action: Before sharing one piece of news today, check whether it is true and necessary to share; if not, leave it unsent.
missions.reflection: Have I ever believed something just because many people repeated it?
missions.vocabulary: Tabayyun — careful verification   •   Naba’ — important news
missions.careNote: Do not ask children to investigate misconduct alone. For accusations, bullying or abuse, route to a trusted adult and never discourage safe reporting.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:6 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/6

missions.title: Loving What Is Right

ayahs.arabic: وَٱعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّ فِيكُمْ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ ۚ لَوْ يُطِيعُكُمْ فِى كَثِيرٍ مِّنَ ٱلْأَمْرِ لَعَنِتُّمْ وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱللَّهَ حَبَّبَ إِلَيْكُمُ ٱلْإِيمَـٰنَ وَزَيَّنَهُۥ فِى قُلُوبِكُمْ وَكَرَّهَ إِلَيْكُمُ ٱلْكُفْرَ وَٱلْفُسُوقَ وَٱلْعِصْيَانَ ۚ أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلرَّٰشِدُونَ  ﴿7﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah's Messenger was among the believers, and Allah made faith dear to them and wrongdoing hateful. Rushing to impose personal ideas would bring hardship.

ayahs.arabic: فَضْلًا مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَنِعْمَةً ۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ  ﴿8﴾
ayahs.meaning: This love of faith is a favor and blessing from Allah, Who knows and is wise.

options: Thank Allah and keep improving without boasting.
Tell everyone you are better than them.
Stop helping because one deed is enough.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:7 / 49:8    |    TRAIT: Gratitude • Humility • Love of faith
missions.aim: Recognize that loving good and avoiding wrongdoing is a blessing from Allah.
missions.tafsir: The passage reminds the early believers that the Messenger ﷺ was among them and warns them against assuming he should always follow their preferred opinions. Allah describes having made faith beloved to their hearts and unbelief, disobedience and rebellion hateful to them. The following verse calls this guidance Allah's grace and favor. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the love of faith as divine guidance, not simply self-congratulation for outward behavior. For children this becomes a gentle lesson in gratitude: when we enjoy praying, tell the truth, or make peace, we should thank Allah rather than boast that we are better than other people. Developing good habits takes help, practice and forgiveness when we slip.
missions.story: After school, Imaan chose to return a colorful pencil case she had found. Akhlaq said, 'You must be the best student in the class!' Imaan smiled but shook her head. 'I am happy I did the right thing, but I don't know who is best. Allah helped me remember what is right.' Later, Akhlaq returned a borrowed ruler without being reminded. He felt the same warm happiness. Their father explained that loving a good action is a gift worth thanking Allah for. That evening, they both made a quiet Du'a for hearts that enjoy what is right.
missions.question: After doing a good deed, what attitude is most fitting?
missions.feedback: Guidance is a gift from Allah; gratitude helps goodness grow without pride.
missions.action: After completing one good deed today, quietly thank Allah without boasting to others.
missions.reflection: What good action has become easier for me recently?
missions.vocabulary: Iman — faith   •   Fadl — grace or favor
missions.careNote: No child should be labeled a “better believer” based on app points. This is an analogy for gratitude, not a measurement of faith.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:7, 8 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/7

missions.title: Becoming a Peacemaker

ayahs.arabic: وَإِن طَآئِفَتَانِ مِنَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ ٱقْتَتَلُوا۟ فَأَصْلِحُوا۟ بَيْنَهُمَا ۖ فَإِنۢ بَغَتْ إِحْدَىٰهُمَا عَلَى ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ فَقَـٰتِلُوا۟ ٱلَّتِى تَبْغِى حَتَّىٰ تَفِىٓءَ إِلَىٰٓ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ ۚ فَإِن فَآءَتْ فَأَصْلِحُوا۟ بَيْنَهُمَا بِٱلْعَدْلِ وَأَقْسِطُوٓا۟ ۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُقْسِطِينَ  ﴿9﴾
ayahs.meaning: When two groups of believers fight, seek reconciliation; if one persists in aggression, lawful authority must restore justice, and reconciliation must be fair.

options: Push both sides apart personally.
Find a responsible adult immediately.
Choose a side and shout louder.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:9    |    TRAIT: Justice • Fair reconciliation • Seeking help
missions.aim: Recognize that reconciliation must be fair and that serious conflict belongs with responsible adults.
missions.tafsir: The verse first calls for reconciliation when groups of believers are in conflict. It then addresses aggression and the need to restore justice before reestablishing peace. Classical Tafsir treats these matters seriously within communal order and lawful authority, not as a child's permission to intervene physically. Al-Tafsir al-Munir discusses settling internal disputes and acting with justice. A child-friendly application is limited to minor disagreements: calmly listen, avoid taking sides blindly, and involve a teacher when necessary. Fighting, threats and coercion must be handed to adults. The Qur'anic principle is more than 'stop arguing': justice matters, and peace should not hide mistreatment.
missions.story: Two friends argued about who should use the playground ball first. As voices rose, some classmates started cheering for a fight. Imaan asked them to stop shouting and suggested asking the sports teacher to help. The teacher learned that one group had been waiting their turn and another had not understood the schedule. They agreed on fair rotations. Later, when Akhlaq noticed older students threatening a younger child, he did not try to confront them alone; he quickly informed the supervising teacher. Imaan told him, 'Helping make peace also means getting the right help when someone is not safe.' Their playground became calmer because fairness was part of the solution.
missions.question: A disagreement starts turning into pushing and threats. What should a child do?
missions.feedback: Safety first. Justice and peacemaking require trusted adults in situations involving harm.
missions.action: Help solve one small disagreement fairly today, or ask a trusted adult to help if it becomes unsafe.
missions.reflection: What is the difference between making peace and pretending nothing wrong happened?
missions.vocabulary: Islah — making things right   •   Adl — justice
missions.careNote: Do not animate or gamify the verse’s armed-conflict elements for young learners. Maintain the literal Quranic context in adult notes.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:9 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/9

missions.title: The Bond of Brotherhood

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّمَا ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ إِخْوَةٌ فَأَصْلِحُوا۟ بَيْنَ أَخَوَيْكُمْ ۚ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُرْحَمُونَ  ﴿10﴾
ayahs.meaning: The believers are brothers in faith; make peace between them and be mindful of Allah so that you may receive mercy.

options: Listen to both, admit mistakes, and agree on a fair way forward.
Remind them of every old argument.
Pressure the hurt child to pretend nothing happened.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:10    |    TRAIT: Brotherhood • Mercy • Reconciliation
missions.aim: Practise reconciling classmates while understanding the special bond of believers.
missions.tafsir: Verse 10 states that believers are brothers and instructs them to make peace between their brothers while fearing Allah. The immediate background follows the previous verse about conflict among believers. Al-Tabari explains the bond of faith and the obligation to seek reconciliation rather than nurse hostility. Children should learn that this is a religious bond, not an excuse to exclude or be unkind to others. A school-friendly application includes restoring a friendship, admitting fault and inviting fair conversation. Reconciliation should not be forced where safety or serious bullying is involved. Forgiveness and making amends can take time.
missions.story: Mohsin and Akhlaq stopped talking after a game in which both thought the other had cheated. Their classmates began choosing teams, making the disagreement bigger. Imaan met them in the reading corner with their teacher nearby. She invited each to explain what happened without interruptions. Both discovered that the rules had never been clear. Akhlaq said, 'I should not have called you a cheater.' Mohsin answered, 'I am sorry I shouted.' They agreed on new rules and returned to the game. No one won a prize for being right; they gained something better by repairing their friendship.
missions.question: Two friends want to make up after a misunderstanding. What helps most?
missions.feedback: Reconciliation brings care and fairness together. Repair takes honesty, not pressure.
missions.action: Offer one sincere peace-making gesture today, such as apologizing for your own mistake or speaking kindly to someone after a disagreement.
missions.reflection: Can I say “I was wrong” without trying to blame someone else?
missions.careNote: Preserve the specifically believing-community meaning of the ayah while encouraging universal courtesy toward classmates.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:10 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/10

missions.title: The Nickname That Hurt

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِّن قَوْمٍ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَكُونُوا۟ خَيْرًا مِّنْهُمْ وَلَا نِسَآءٌ مِّن نِّسَآءٍ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَكُنَّ خَيْرًا مِّنْهُنَّ ۖ وَلَا تَلْمِزُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا۟ بِٱلْأَلْقَـٰبِ ۖ بِئْسَ ٱلِٱسْمُ ٱلْفُسُوقُ بَعْدَ ٱلْإِيمَـٰنِ ۚ وَمَن لَّمْ يَتُبْ فَأُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلظَّـٰلِمُونَ  ﴿11﴾
ayahs.meaning: Do not mock, insult, or call one another hurtful names. The person being mocked may be better before Allah. Turn away from wrongdoing.

options: Continue because friends are laughing.
Stop, use the person’s preferred name, and apologize for earlier teasing.
Tell the child to become less sensitive.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:11    |    TRAIT: Dignity • Kind speech • Repentance
missions.aim: Stop teasing and hurtful nicknames, and learn to repair harm through sincere apologies.
missions.tafsir: Allah prohibits believers from mocking one another, insulting each other, and calling one another offensive names. The verse warns that the person mocked may be better before Allah than the one doing the mocking, and ends by calling people to repentance. Al-Tabari interprets the prohibition broadly rather than limiting it to a single class or reason for ridicule. This covers poverty, appearance, family circumstances, errors, language, and any other pretext for making someone feel small. For children, joking is not harmless merely because several people laugh; the target's dignity matters. If a child has mocked someone, repentance should include stopping, apologizing, and not repeating the injury.
missions.story: A new student, Naseer, pronounced one classroom word differently. A few children began repeating the pronunciation in a silly voice. Akhlaq laughed once, but then saw Naseer's face. During break, Imaan asked, 'Would you like it if people kept saying your name wrongly?' Akhlaq realized the joke was hurting someone. He approached Naseer and apologized without adding 'but it was only a joke.' The next morning he used Naseer's proper name and invited him into the group game. Over the week, the teasing stopped, and Naseer felt more comfortable speaking in class.
missions.question: A nickname makes a classmate uncomfortable. What should Akhlaq do?
missions.feedback: Allah teaches believers to protect dignity. A sincere apology is stronger than a clever insult.
missions.action: Use everyone’s respectful name today; if you have teased someone, offer a genuine apology.
missions.reflection: What makes a joke kind rather than cruel?
missions.vocabulary: Sukhriyah — mockery   •   Tawbah — turning back in repentance
missions.careNote: Do not create punishments or embarrassing peer ratings. For ongoing bullying, adult support is necessary.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:11 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/11

missions.title: The Secret That Was Shared

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱجْتَنِبُوا۟ كَثِيرًا مِّنَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِنَّ بَعْضَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ ۖ وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا۟ وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا ۚ أَيُحِبُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن يَأْكُلَ لَحْمَ أَخِيهِ مَيْتًا فَكَرِهْتُمُوهُ ۚ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ تَوَّابٌ رَّحِيمٌ  ﴿12﴾
ayahs.meaning: Avoid much unfounded suspicion, do not spy, and do not speak badly about people behind their backs. Fear Allah, Who accepts repentance and is merciful.

options: Read it quietly so no one notices.
Create an even more interesting rumor.
Respect their privacy and redirect the conversation.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:12    |    TRAIT: Privacy • Fair assumptions • Protecting reputations
missions.aim: Avoid unsupported accusations, spying, and speaking badly about people behind their backs.
missions.tafsir: The verse prohibits much suspicious thinking when it lacks good grounds, warns against spying, and forbids backbiting. Its striking Qur'anic image communicates the ugliness of speaking about someone's faults behind their back; for young children the image should not be visualized frighteningly. Ibn Kathir draws attention to the ban on distrust and spying, connecting the command with authentic Hadith about avoiding suspicion. A child can learn to separate a fact from an unkind guess, and to leave private diaries and messages alone. At the same time, telling a trusted adult about danger or abuse is not prohibited backbiting: the aim is to seek protection, not to humiliate someone.
missions.story: Imaan noticed a folded note sticking out of Mohsina's schoolbag. Akhlaq said, 'Maybe it tells us why she was absent.' He reached toward it. Imaan gently stopped him. 'That belongs to Mohsina.' Later, some classmates guessed that Mohsina had skipped school without permission. The teacher explained that her family had been caring for an ill relative. Akhlaq felt glad they had not opened the note or repeated those guesses. At lunch, he turned the conversation toward a class project instead of discussing someone who was not there. He was learning that a friend's private life is not a puzzle for others to solve.
missions.question: Friends want to read another child’s private note and share theories about them. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Privacy and reputations deserve protection. If someone is unsafe, tell a trustworthy adult rather than keeping a dangerous secret.
missions.action: Protect one person’s privacy today by not peeking at or sharing something that is not yours to disclose.
missions.reflection: How can I talk about someone fairly when they are not present?
missions.vocabulary: Ghibah — speaking about an absent person in a way they would dislike   •   Tajassus — spying
missions.careNote: Do not show the verse’s graphic metaphor as an animation. Clarify the difference between gossip and safety disclosure.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:12 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/12

missions.title: Different Families, Equal Dignity

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَـٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلْنَـٰكُمْ شُعُوبًا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتْقَىٰكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌ  ﴿13﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah created humanity from a male and a female and formed peoples and tribes so we may know one another. Honor before Allah rests on Taqwa, not lineage.

options: Laugh at the accent.
Welcome the student and learn to pronounce their name respectfully.
Avoid the student because they are different.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:13    |    TRAIT: Human dignity • Taqwa • Getting to know others
missions.aim: Recognize that people’s backgrounds are not measures of worth and that Taqwa matters to Allah.
missions.tafsir: Allah addresses humanity as a whole, saying He created people from a male and female and made them peoples and tribes so they could know one another. The verse declares that the most honored in Allah's sight is the most mindful of Him. Ibn Kathir explains shared human origin and that lineage alone is not a measure of spiritual superiority. For children this clearly rejects mocking language, complexion, nationality, dialect, wealth or family background. It also keeps the verse's explicit theological claim: honor before Allah is tied to Taqwa, not to a vague claim that all beliefs are identical. Only Allah knows hearts fully, so children should not rank classmates' faith. Being curious and respectful toward others is a practical expression of the verse's teaching.
missions.story: The class held a 'family stories' day. Children brought pictures of hometowns, recipes, and words spoken at home. Akhlaq liked learning a new greeting from Mohsin, while Naseer described mountains near his grandparents' home. One child joked that a particular accent sounded strange. Imaan invited everyone to imagine how hard it can be to learn a new language. The group tried saying the greetings respectfully and began asking thoughtful questions. Their teacher reminded them that Allah made people into different communities so they could know one another. By the end, every child had learned something new, and nobody needed to feel ashamed of their background.
missions.question: A new student speaks with a different accent. What response follows the lesson best?
missions.feedback: Differences help us get to know one another. Allah values Taqwa rather than appearance or ancestry.
missions.action: Learn one respectful fact about someone with a different family or cultural background without making assumptions.
missions.reflection: What is one good quality I can appreciate in someone different from me?
missions.vocabulary: Shu’ub — peoples   •   Taqwa — mindful obedience to Allah
missions.careNote: Keep explicit Qur’anic criterion of Taqwa. Do not imply children can judge which peer is most righteous.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:13 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/13

missions.title: Faith Beyond Words

ayahs.arabic: قَالَتِ ٱلْأَعْرَابُ ءَامَنَّا ۖ قُل لَّمْ تُؤْمِنُوا۟ وَلَـٰكِن قُولُوٓا۟ أَسْلَمْنَا وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ ٱلْإِيمَـٰنُ فِى قُلُوبِكُمْ ۖ وَإِن تُطِيعُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ لَا يَلِتْكُم مِّنْ أَعْمَـٰلِكُمْ شَيْـًٔا ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ  ﴿14﴾
ayahs.meaning: Some desert Arabs claimed complete faith, but they were told that outward submission had occurred while deep faith had not yet entered their hearts; Allah is forgiving and merciful.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّمَا ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَرْتَابُوا۟ وَجَـٰهَدُوا۟ بِأَمْوَٰلِهِمْ وَأَنفُسِهِمْ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ ۚ أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلصَّـٰدِقُونَ  ﴿15﴾
ayahs.meaning: True believers have faith in Allah and His Messenger, do not doubt, and strive sincerely with what they possess for Allah's cause.

options: Claim he did it.
Admit the mistake and make a realistic plan to finish.
Blame a classmate without evidence.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:14 / 49:15    |    TRAIT: Sincerity • Faith in action • Perseverance
missions.aim: Understand that saying a good thing and sincerely living by it are different, and that only Allah fully knows hearts.
missions.tafsir: Verse 14 addresses certain desert Arabs who claimed the full station of faith, while the verse distinguishes outward Islam from deep Iman in the heart. Verse 15 describes genuine believers as those whose faith is not accompanied by doubt and who strive sincerely with their means for Allah's cause. Ibn Kathir discusses this distinction by referring to the well-known differentiation of Islam and Iman. For children, the right lesson is personal sincerity, not policing who is a 'real Muslim'. The references to striving are part of the verse's full scriptural wording and should be explained by qualified teachers in original context, not converted into games of confrontation. Daily applications may include keeping a promise, sincere prayer, and supporting good causes within a child's ability.
missions.story: At school, the children were asked to care for a new bookshelf. Akhlaq promised to arrange the books neatly, but soon became interested in a game instead. When the teacher asked, he almost said, 'Of course I did it.' He paused and admitted that he had not completed the task. Imaan offered to help him finish after class. 'I want to be someone whose actions match his words,' he said. Their teacher explained that sincerity grows when we speak truthfully, admit our weaknesses and try again. That evening Akhlaq finished a smaller responsibility at home without being reminded. It felt better than boasting about a task he had not done.
missions.question: Akhlaq promised to finish a task but forgot. What is the most sincere response?
missions.feedback: Sincerity is shown through honesty and effort, not by pretending to be perfect.
missions.action: Keep one small promise today; if you cannot, tell the truth and make it right.
missions.reflection: What is one part of my character I want to strengthen quietly?
missions.careNote: Do not turn 49:14–15 into a religious-identity quiz or call children hypocrites. Historic and theological distinctions require adult guidance.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:14, 15 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/14

missions.title: The Gift of Guidance

ayahs.arabic: قُلْ أَتُعَلِّمُونَ ٱللَّهَ بِدِينِكُمْ وَٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۚ وَٱللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمٌ  ﴿16﴾
ayahs.meaning: Do people imagine they can inform Allah about their faith? Allah already knows everything in the heavens and earth.

ayahs.arabic: يَمُنُّونَ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ أَسْلَمُوا۟ ۖ قُل لَّا تَمُنُّوا۟ عَلَىَّ إِسْلَـٰمَكُم ۖ بَلِ ٱللَّهُ يَمُنُّ عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ هَدَىٰكُمْ لِلْإِيمَـٰنِ إِن كُنتُمْ صَـٰدِقِينَ  ﴿17﴾
ayahs.meaning: Some counted their becoming Muslim as a favor to the Prophet ﷺ. In reality, Allah's guidance to faith is the favor bestowed upon them.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ غَيْبَ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۚ وَٱللَّهُ بَصِيرٌۢ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ  ﴿18﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah knows what is unseen in the heavens and on earth, and sees all that people do.

options: Stop helping until someone praises you.
Say you are better than everyone else.
Be grateful to Allah and keep doing good.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-HUJURAT • 49:16 / 49:17 / 49:18    |    TRAIT: Humility • Thankfulness • Integrity
missions.aim: Understand that Allah knows what people do and that guidance is His gift, not something we can boast about.
missions.tafsir: The final verses reject the idea that people can teach Allah about their inner beliefs. They also correct those who counted their acceptance of Islam as a favor to the Messenger ﷺ: true guidance is Allah's grace to them. Allah knows unseen realities and sees actions. Al-Tabari explains that Allah knows what is hidden in hearts, including what people reveal and conceal. Children may learn humility here: we do not have to advertise every good deed; we can be grateful that Allah helps us do right. This is not a license for adults to shame children by claiming to know their intentions. Allah alone knows the unseen. Present the ending as a hopeful invitation to honesty, gratitude, and lifelong improvement.
missions.story: Imaan helped a younger child find a missing water bottle. She almost announced the story to everyone, hoping for praise. Then she saw that the child was smiling and already felt safe. She quietly returned to her work. Later, Akhlaq asked, 'Didn't you want everyone to know?' Imaan answered, 'It was enough to help. Allah knows.' They talked with their father about how guidance itself is a gift, and how even good deeds should not become a reason to look down on others. Before bed, each quietly remembered one blessing from the day. Neither needed a badge to make the good deed meaningful.
missions.question: You have helped someone and nobody notices. What is a beautiful response?
missions.feedback: Allah knows what is hidden and sees our actions. Sincere goodness does not need applause.
missions.action: Do one small helpful deed today without asking anyone to praise you.
missions.reflection: What gift from Allah am I most grateful for today?
missions.careNote: The unseen belongs to Allah. Do not frame caregiver surveillance or app telemetry as “Allah watching” and avoid anxiety-inducing visuals.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 49:16, 17, 18 • Tafsir: al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/49/16
